He speaks here of another sin, which is theft, and chooses from it the hardest, which is stealing a man and selling him as a slave; this is a contempt for a man's life that approaches the sin of murder, so the Law sentences this thief to death.

Do not steal the rights of others to express their opinion or their freedom of movement, life and choice, even if your aim is good, because God Himself does not force His children to live with Him but calls them to Him in every way, in addition to the fact that man cannot bear the loss of his freedom all his life.

He points here to another sin, which is cursing when it is directed at the nearest of kin, the parents; it is an insult and a robbing of their honor, so it also approaches the sin of murder, therefore the Law sentences the curser to death.

Do not persist in your anger so that words insulting to others come out of your mouth, for by this you kill them morally and not physically, and this too is a hard matter and leads to many psychological troubles. So do not be lax in this, relying on their being members of your household or under your authority, for this is a hard sin before God and its punishment is great. And remember that your basic work is to encourage others to draw near to God and to do constructive work.

He returns again to the sin of striking, using any means such as a stick or stones; if that leads to the other's death, the striker is put to death, as mentioned in (v. 12), but if he is sick for a time in his house, the striker is not put to death but compensates the one struck by paying his wages for the days of his being kept from work and also the cost of his treatment.

If you have wronged a person you must compensate him for the harm of your wronging him. If you insulted him with words of cursing, you must apologize to him, and if the insult was in front of people, the apology should also be in front of people, and if any material harm befell him, he must be compensated more than what befell him; this is a proof of your repentance and your love.

The law of striking included masters with their servants, so out of sanctification of man's life, even if he is a servant, if his striking by his master led to his death, vengeance is taken on his master. What is meant by vengeance is his punishment, and most likely his being put to death or his paying a large fine, as the judges or elders decide. The Gentiles considered the servant part of the master's property and held that it was his right to kill him if he wished.

If a master strikes his servant and he lives a day or two, vengeance is not taken on him, first because he did not intend to kill him and second because his material loss in losing his servant is enough for him.
But in the first case, which is the death of the servant, vengeance is taken on the master because he went beyond discipline in his striking and was violent to the point of killing.

If a quarrel occurs between men and they strike a woman with child so that her unborn child comes out, its growth not having been completed inside her womb, this is considered a sin of killing without intent but of a human being not yet complete, therefore the men are not put to death and do not flee to the cities of refuge, but they pay a fine as the judges decide, after the husband demands what he wants.

This is a sin of negligence and violent anger that led to a fight, therefore the wrongdoer is punished with a fine according to the circumstances of each case and the extent of the harm that occurred and the violence of the quarrel.

If the men's colliding with the woman with child led to her falling and dying, those who struck her are put to death; this is a sin of killing without intent but connected with the sin of violent anger that led to a quarrel which ended a human life, so it is different from the sin of killing without intent mentioned in (v. 13) because it is connected with violent anger.

If harm is done to the woman with child by the quarrelers and one of her members is injured or lost, such as the eye, the tooth, the hand or the foot, then whoever struck her is punished by having his eye put out or one of his teeth, or his hand or foot cut off, and he may compensate by a suitable fine as the judges decide.
And this law declares justice and the bearing of responsibility, so that man may take care not to harm another, or he will be punished with the same harm.
St. Augustine divided dealings between people into five degrees, which are:
1- Attacking the other and harming him, and this is what happens among barbarous peoples.
2- Wronging the wrongdoer with a greater harm because he is the one who began.
3- Wronging the wrongdoer with the same amount of harm that he caused, as in Judaism.
4- Wronging the wrongdoer and harming him with a lesser harm, and this is what happens among higher peoples, if the one who was wronged is distressed and expresses his distress with some wrong.
5- Forgiving the wrongdoer and pitying him as a sick man, and even offering him love, and this is the highest conduct, as in Christianity.

And this law points to the matter of redemption, since every harm needs a like compensation, and man's unlimited sin needs unlimited atonement and unlimited compensation, and this was accomplished in Christ's death for us on the Cross. By this law the victim was prevented from taking vengeance beyond the harm that befell him: if his eye was injured, for example, he does not take vengeance by more than hurting the other's eye. But what used to happen in any attack was that the elders would estimate the amount of the injury and fine the attacker the suitable price, which he pays to the victim (Num 35:21-25).
He continues the kinds of harm and the compensation for them with their equivalents, which are:
1- Whoever uses a hot metal tool to burn the skin of another (a brand) is dealt with as he has done.
2- Whoever wounds another so that blood flows from him is punished with the same punishment.
3- Whoever strikes another so that bruises (contusions) occur is struck until like bruises occur on him.
If a master strikes his servant and causes him to lose his eye or one of his teeth, then in compensation for this harm he lets him go free.

If a person approaches an ox without caution and it gores him and he dies, the ox is put to death, to show the importance of human life, but the owner of the ox is not punished because he intended no evil, and it was the one killed who approached the ox without care. And the flesh of the ox is not eaten, because it was not slaughtered in the natural way but was killed by stoning, so its blood is in it, and it signifies aggression and evil.

Care about the lives and feelings of others more than about your property and your comfort. Do not be selfish and cause harm unintentionally through your preoccupation with your work or your trade or your personal mood, such as making noise or exploiting your ability in trade so that you press on others until they lose their trade entirely; rather, be merciful and consider the feelings of others.

If the ox was one that often gored and had harmed others before, and its owner was warned by many and did not restrain it or slaughter it but left it to harm others until it killed a person, the Law decrees that the ox be put to death and its owner also, because he despises the lives of people and is immersed in his selfishness, caring about his property more than about the lives of others.

If the relatives of the one killed agree to accept a ransom for the dead man, then as the elders estimate, the owner must pay this fine as compensation for the killing of the person whom the ox gored.

If the one killed by the ox's goring is young in age, his life is not made light of because of his youth, but the owner of the ox is put to death if his ox was one that often gored and he had been warned, with the killing of the ox; but if the ox was not a goring one, only the ox is put to death.
A shekel of silver: equal to about 360 g - 450 g of silver.

If the ox gores a manservant or a maidservant and kills him, the master is compensated with the price of the servant, which is thirty shekels of silver, and the ox is stoned to death, to show the importance of human life.

If a person is negligent, having opened one of the old wells for drinking and after drinking from it did not cover it with a stone, or if he dug a new well and after drinking from it did not cover it with a stone, and one of the animals such as an ox or an ass fell into it, this negligent person is punished by paying a fine, which is the price of this ox or ass, and this negligent person takes the dead animal to benefit from its hide or its fleece or anything in it.

Beware of negligence that harms others, whether in your work or your speech, and if it happens you must compensate, and an apology is not enough; and as you want others not to neglect you, do not neglect them either.

If an ox gores another animal such as another ox and it dies, the ox that gored is sold and they divide its price, that is, the owner of the ox that gored and the owner of the ox that was killed, and likewise the dead ox is sold and they divide its price.

If an ox gores another ox and it is known that the ox was a goring one and its owner was warned before witnesses and did nothing, he is punished by compensating the owner of the dead ox by giving him an ox like it, and then this negligent man takes the dead ox to benefit from its remains.
Laws of theft, adultery, cursing and other laws

Since the eighth commandment forbade theft, here God decrees the penalty for the one who steals, which is restitution of four or five times as much, as a kind of discipline for the thief and to show the seriousness of the effect of his theft on others, by bringing fear and disturbance upon them, so that he must compensate them with more than he stole from them. And if the size and price of what was stolen increases, the compensation is greater (five oxen - four sheep). The greater the thief's greed, the greater the discipline he needs, with greater compensation, because the one who steals an ox is bolder in evil than others, besides the fact that he deprived its owners of the price of hiring it out or of using it in work, so the compensation for his theft is greater.

May you think about the effects of your sins on others so that you turn back from them, and then try to make up to others, not only with an apology but with words and deeds of love, so that you restore to them trust in you and peace of mind in dealing with you.

If the thief breaks through the wall or the door during the act of theft, and the owner of the goods senses him, rises to defend himself and strikes the thief so that he dies, the thief deserves this death because of his evil, and the owner of the house is not avenged upon or punished, because he was defending his property.

The sun be risen upon him: the thief continued trying to steal until daybreak, and then the owner of the goods can call to his neighbors and they can seize the thief, so he has no need to kill him in self-defense.
There shall be blood shed for him: that is, he is alive and can be seized alive, and it is not lawful to kill him.

He should make full restitution: the thief is punished by making restitution for what he was trying to steal. Since he had not taken it, slaughtered it or sold it, it says only that he shall make restitution and does not specify the amount of the restitution; this is determined by the judges, and it is usually double. If he have nothing: if he is poor and destitute.

Then he shall be sold for his theft: he is sold as a slave to the owner of the goods or to someone else, and the owner of the goods takes the price; and it is the right of the owner of the goods, if he takes him as a slave, to sell him to whomever he wishes if he does not see fit to keep him with him. This calls for not being hasty in killing the thief, and decrees that he be punished with restitution, and even if he is destitute, he sells himself as a slave to the owner of the goods.

If the thief is caught with the stolen goods in his hand and has not disposed of them by slaughtering or selling them, that is, he has not gone further in his greed and theft, he is disciplined by paying lesser compensation, which is double.

Here he speaks of unintentional theft that results from negligence, in the case of the shepherd who lets his sheep eat from his neighbor's field. Here he must compensate his neighbor with the best fruits of his own field, because he could have kept the sheep away but was merely negligent, that is, he took what was not his, namely the fruits of his brother's field.
If fire break out, and catch in thorns: if thorns or any wood or goods burn in someone's field.

So that the stacks of corn burn: the fire moved with the wind from the burning thorns to the neighbor's storehouses, where he keeps goods piled one upon another, of grain or anything else, and these stores burned. Or the standing corn, or the field: that is, crops that had begun to dry, or any goods that were in the field.

He that kindled the fire shall surely make restitution: the one who lit the fire and did not take care that it should not reach his neighbor is responsible for this negligence, and the judges decide on the appropriate compensation; but it will be less than for the one who was negligent with his sheep eating his neighbor's crops, because keeping sheep away is easier than stopping a fire.

If a man deliver to another silver or goods to keep as a trust for someone else, and it is stolen, and the thief is caught, this thief makes restitution of double only, because the stolen goods were found with him and he had not disposed of them.
If it is impossible to catch the thief, the one who was keeping the trust is brought before the judges to examine whether he stole this trust or it was stolen from him.
The cause of both parties: the one who deposited and the one with whom it was deposited, or the thief and the one robbed.

In the end he decrees the summary of the law of restitution, which is that anything stolen that is found with the thief is compensated for with two, after the judges examine him and decide that he is the thief. That is, if the one with whom the thing was deposited denies the deposited thing and his guilt is proved, he pays double; and the one who found something lost and denied it pays the owner of the lost thing double. And bringing their cause before God means bringing it before the elders so that they may judge who is the thief.

If a man delivers to another a trust such as an animal, and it dies, or is hurt, or is stolen from him, the owner of the animal and the trustee are brought to the court, and if it is proved that the trustee did not interfere, the owner of the animal receives no compensation at all, because he was faithful over the animal.
No man seeing it: there was no witness who saw what happened to the animal.
The oath of the LORD: he raises his right hand and swears by the truth.

If the animal deposited with the trustee is stolen because he was careless in guarding it, he makes restitution for it since it was stolen, because he was negligent in watching over it. But if it was stolen while grazing in the wilderness by some passing traveler without the trustee seeing, he makes no compensation at all, as stated in (v. 10).

If a wild beast attacks the deposited animal and kills it, the trustee presents evidence proving that it was torn, which is the testimony of witnesses or parts of the animal's body that the beast left behind, and this evidence is presented to the court, so the owner of the animal receives no compensation.

If a person borrows anything and it is lost or broken, and the owner of this thing is rich and not in need, he does not compensate him for what was damaged. But if the owner of the thing is in need, the borrower must compensate him.

And if a man hires anything and the thing he hired is lost or broken, he does not compensate its owner, because he paid the hire for this thing, and this hire compensates for any damage that may occur.
Entice: he showed affection for the purpose of fornication.

If a man approaches a virgin and influences her emotionally until he commits fornication with her, he must bear his responsibility, marry her, and pay her father the dowry, the amount customarily paid in such cases according to custom and society, which is fifty shekels of silver (Deut 22:29). It is noted that this amount is more than the usual amount in a dowry because he sinned against a virgin; and if he marries her, he does not divorce her, that is, he is bound to his new marriage. Here he deals with the problem through a positive act, which is marriage.

But if the girl was betrothed and committed fornication with the man of her own will, both are stoned; but if the man raped her, that is, she was the one wronged, the man who assaulted her is stoned alone (Deut 22:23-27).
If a man commits fornication with a virgin and wants to marry her but her father refuses, he is bound to pay the dowry as compensation for his offense against her.

Sorcery is considered dealing with demons and submission to them, and it also draws souls to deal with them; so it is spiritual fornication and a promotion of fornication by causing others to fall. That is, sorcery is a rejection of faith in God and a resort to another power, which is Satan, the adversary of God; therefore the Law commands that sorcerers be put to death. It says "a witch" because most of those who practiced sorcery at that time were women (1 Sam 28:7, Acts 16:16).

The sin of causing others to stumble is a hideous sin, for it makes others fall into evil; so instead of a person striving for good and drawing souls to God, he makes light of them and of their salvation. Therefore be careful in your words and actions so that you do not cause anyone to stumble.

Fornication with animals is not an offense against a human being, but it is uncleanness and immersion in bodily pleasure. This sin was widespread among the Canaanites, among whom the children of Israel lived; therefore whoever does this is put to death, because it is considered uncleanness, it angers God, and it deserves death.

It is understood from this verse that uncleanness is an evil that greatly angers God, even if neither party complains; so if two agree to commit fornication, God is angry at their evil because it is uncleanness.
The worship of idols is spiritual fornication; therefore whoever does it is punished by death.

Do not exploit the stranger, because he knows no one in the place, so that you trouble him or oppress him and demand of him more than his duties; for lack of mercy greatly displeases God. And so that God may stir their feelings of mercy, He reminds them that they were strangers in Egypt for many long years, so that, recalling how hard the feelings of being a stranger are, they may have mercy on strangers.

The widow is the woman without a husband, that is, without support, and the fatherless is the one without a father, that is, without care; and so they always signify the need for mercy. Therefore wronging them is harder than wronging any ordinary person, and is considered a great injustice.

Care for the weak and the needy, have compassion on them, help them and bear with them because of their hard circumstances. And do not forget that you are the widow who has no support but God, and the fatherless who has no true father but God, and the stranger in this world who is poor of every virtue, so that you may be humbled and seek God's mercies, and this will move you to be merciful to everyone.

God declares His fatherhood and care for the weak in His attention to the prayers of the oppressed, such as the widow and the fatherless. If your oppression of the widow and the fatherless increases, He is angry with you, and enemies attack and kill the men, so that your wives become widows and your children fatherless, because you did not have compassion on the widow and the fatherless.

Another form of mercy is lending to the needy. He requires His people not to charge usury, that is, any interest on the amount borrowed, but it is enough that they take back the same amount, sharing with the needy person in the amount of interest they have given up. And of course, if feelings of mercy are stirred, a person can lend and not demand that the other repay what he borrowed; and it is better to help the needy from the beginning with the amount as a gift. Debts were released by their owner when the seventh year came (Deut 15:11-17), and it was permitted for the Jews to take usury from non-Jews (Deut 23:19, 20). But sadly the Jews abandoned this law, as is shown by what happened in the days of Elisha the prophet with the widow woman (2 Kgs 4:1).
Raiment: this is the outer garment that covers his body and keeps him warm during the night if he has no other covering.

If a poor man is compelled to pledge his garment because of his need for money, and walked naked that day and could not repay what he owed within the day, then before the going down of the sun, that is, after he has worked and received his wages and still could not repay, the one who took the garment must return it to him so that he may sleep in it, for how can he sleep naked when he may have no covering? And if he wrongs him and keeps the garment with him, then in his distress and need he cries out to God, and then He hears him, because He is merciful, and takes vengeance on the one who wronged him for exploiting the poor man.

God's mercies toward the needy also appear in what the Law prescribes, that it is not permitted to take a widow's garment in pledge because of her particular circumstances, but she borrows without pledging anything (Deut 24:17).

Another form of oppression is abuse. However troubled a person may be, he must not dare to revile God or the ruler of his people, but must endure, and he will understand afterward the reason for the affliction he is passing through, and perhaps the reason is his sin.
Man goes on and on in the sin of oppression, and is not content with oppressing human beings but dares to oppress God also:

First: by reviling God while murmuring (v. 28). Then, in this verse, by not offering the firstfruits, whether of the grain gathered on the threshing floor, or of the grapes and olives pressed in the winepress, or of the firstborn sons, for whom a ransom is offered, as mentioned in (ch. 13:13).

Likewise God requires them to offer the firstborn of animals such as cattle and sheep, and God's mercy appears in that the animal is taken only after seven days, so that it may suckle from its mother the basic milk that nourishes it, and out of respect for the mother's motherhood toward her suckling; this is compassion for the animal.

Offer the firstfruits and the tithes to receive God's blessing on all your possessions, and know that God does not need your gifts, but they are so that you may show your love for God, your sympathy with the poor and your care for the needs of the Church, and God will repay you with many blessings.
He forbids them to eat an animal torn by beasts, because it is unclean for two reasons:
(1) That it has been touched by an unclean animal, which is the predatory animal.
(2) That its blood did not come out of it but was held in it, so it becomes unclean.
And He commands them to cast it to the dogs. In this He calls them to holiness, not only in eating clean meat but in all their life, so that their hearts may be pure from evil and loving God.
Justice, the feasts, God's presence with them, and refusing to mingle with the wicked

Here He rejects the sin of lying by rejecting false reports, and therefore a person cannot bear false witness, for this is supporting false speech; that is, the Law calls him to reject lying in all its forms.

Do not make light of lying through exaggeration and overstatement or through understatement and belittling, but be careful in all your words and do not be hasty in them, and examine every report you hear, and God will guide you to distinguish truth from falsehood; and do not spread false talk without intending to, leading others astray and angering God.
He also warns against sharing in any evil by word or deed, and against supporting anything false, even if everyone agrees on it.
Do not pity the poor man because of his weak appearance and so pervert justice and wrong the rich man, but be just, and let the poor man be punished if he is in the wrong.

God calls them to help others, not only loved ones and relatives but enemies also. If an animal belonging to one of their enemies strays away from him and is lost and one of the Hebrews finds it, he must take hold of it and bring it back to the enemy. And if this was in the Law of the Old Testament, how much more in the New Testament we must love enemies and have compassion on them.

If your heart is filled with love, you will love every person, even if he wrongs you or is your enemy; for through love you become like Christ, you reach the Kingdom, you put your enemy to shame, and you break the evil that is in you and in him.
Wouldest forbear to help him: you refused to help your enemy.
Thou shalt surely help with him: you must help your enemy.

He gives another example of helping others and chooses an animal, the donkey, which carries loads and belongs to an enemy, and has fallen to the ground on the road under the weight of the load. He requires him to lift the load off the donkey and set it up so that it may continue its way; for lifting such loads is usually not done by one person but by two or more, that is, he helps the one who wrongs him to set his donkey on its feet.

He gives another example of helping others, which is helping the weak, such as the poor man. If he brings a suit before the judges to examine some problem, he must not join the rich in pressing the poor man so that he loses his case because he has no champion on account of his poverty, but must declare the truth and support the poor man and not pervert justice.

In helping others, He calls them to support the innocent and the righteous before the judges, so that he does not lie, that is, bear false witness, and wrong the innocent and kill him and justify the wicked; for God is not pleased with this, because playing with words, that is, lying, can mislead the court so that it wrongs the innocent and justifies the wicked.

Be careful in your words lest you suggest an accusation against the innocent or flatter the wicked because of his position or your embarrassment before him; but proclaim the voice of God gently and clearly even if it does not please the wicked, for God's pleasure with you is more important than people.

He also forbids, in their helping others, bribery, which influences a person to blind him to the truth, so that he looks for crooked ways and loopholes in the law to justify the one who gave him the bribe, and so loses his justice as a judge, since he becomes like a blind man who does not see the truth.

He asks them to help others in the case of strangers who have no support from others, and to remember that they were in need of help when they were strangers in Egypt, from the days of Joseph until Moses.
The Law also commands that the land be sown for six years and then be given rest in the seventh year, for several purposes:
1- The poor eat from it the remains of the crops in it and the natural plants that grow in it.
2- What is left after the poor is eaten by the animals.
3- The land rests from the strain of cultivation to make up for what it has lost and prepare for sowing in the following year, and this is scientifically beneficial.
In addition to the spiritual benefits, which are:
1- Faith in God and reliance on Him, because He promised to give double the harvest in the sixth year, which would suffice their needs for two years.
2- An opportunity to devote themselves to the worship of God in the seventh year.

And when the children of Israel neglected to carry out the commandment of the seventh year, God punished them with captivity, so that by depriving them of their land for seventy years they would make up for what they had neglected in sanctifying the seventh year in the past, before the captivity (2 Chr 36:21).
The stranger: the foreigner who serves you and works for you.

The law of compassion also appears in the law of sanctifying the Sabbath day, for agricultural work is left on the Sabbath, and thus rest is given to the animals working in the cultivation of the land, and likewise to the slaves, in addition to the hired workers he hires from the Gentiles.
Here he summarizes what preceded, confirming the carrying out of the preceding commandments, the most important of which are the worship of God and the rejection of idols.
Here He sets out the three most important feasts of the Jews, which are.

The first feast is the Passover, the cause of their deliverance from the slavery of Egypt, and it is a type of the Lord Christ the crucified Redeemer. And the other two feasts are the harvest and the ingathering; for in the time of material joy we must thank God and glorify Him.
The feasts were mentioned in detail in (Lev 23, Num 18, 28).

The Passover is followed by the feast of unleavened bread, free of leaven, which they eat for seven days, and it signifies purity from all evil, which is signified by leaven. And He requires them to offer God's gifts in this feast as proof of their love for Him, and they keep the feast from the evening of the fourteenth day of the month of Abib (Nisan) until the evening of the twenty-first day of it.
And the month of Abib mentioned corresponds to the months of March and April, and it is different from the Abib found in the Coptic year.
Take care to offer something to God every day through worship and doing good, so that you do not stand before Him empty on this day, and on the last day you will find something to offer Him.

The feast of harvest (or the feast of Pentecost): this is the gathering of the crops that ripen at the beginning of the season, which are the winter crops such as wheat. This feast falls fifty days after the first Sunday after the Passover, and this Sunday was called the feast of firstfruits, and it was mentioned in detail in (Lev 23, Deut 16). The feast of ingathering (which is the feast of tabernacles): in it the crops that ripen late are gathered, that is, the summer crops such as grapes and olives, and its duration is a week beginning on the fifteenth of the seventh month (Ethanim). The people dwell in booths during this period in remembrance of their sojourning in the wilderness of Sinai, and it was mentioned in detail in (Lev 23, Deut 16). In these two feasts each one offers the firstfruits of what God has gathered, that He may bless the rest of the harvest gathered, and they are to be glad because God allowed them to give to Him, and likewise the needy rejoice, who are satisfied by these gifts.

God redeemed the firstborn of the children of Israel with the Passover lamb from the plague on the firstborn; therefore the males owe their lives to God and come in these feasts to thank Him and praise Him.

And the male represents his family and not only himself, so all the males come to keep the feast to God in these feasts. Of course women can also attend, but at least the males attend as representatives of their families to offer their gifts to God and thank Him because He saved them from slavery in Egypt and from death, just as we now thank God in the feasts because He saved us from the death of sin.

He commands them in the feast of the Passover that the sacrifice be accompanied by unleavened bread without leaven, because unleavened bread signifies the purity with which a person comes forward to receive God's salvation.

He also commands them not to leave any of the Passover sacrifice until the next day, as in (ch. 12); and in general the fat of any sacrifice offered to God is burned on the altar of burnt offering, for it is God's, and neither the priest nor the people eat of it, so the fat must be burned on the altar on the day the animal is slaughtered, that is, the part belonging to God is offered immediately after the sacrifice is slaughtered.
The house of the LORD: the tabernacle of the congregation or the temple of Solomon that was built later.

Here He stresses offering the firstfruits. And God's mercy appears in that they are not to boil a kid newly born that is still suckling from its mother; for God teaches us compassion toward animals so that we may have compassion all the more on our poor and weak brethren. In addition, it is His rejection of a pagan belief among the Gentiles that prescribed cooking a newborn kid in its mother's milk and then pouring out its broth on the fields to give fertility to the land. And in general the Law teaches a person not to cook the small slaughtered animal and eat it with its mother's milk, which was supposed to feed it so that it might live by it, so that he may learn compassion in all his dealings.
An Angel: what is meant by the angel here is a messenger, and he is either:
1- A luminous angel who leads them on the way until the Promised Land.
2- An angel who appears in the form of the pillar of fire or the pillar of cloud.

3- God Himself who speaks with them, and what is meant is the Angel of the Covenant, that is, the Second Hypostasis, in the form of a voice speaking or a cloud appearing in the tabernacle of the congregation, showing His presence and being there.
He warns them so that they may obey this Angel, because he represents God or is God Himself, since He says My name is in him, and he will not pardon their sins if they persist in evil.
He promises them that if they obey the Angel, that is, obey God, He will defend them against their enemies, that is, they will walk in assurance in all their life.

He also promises them that the Angel will bring them to the Promised Land and will destroy the wicked peoples dwelling there so that they may dwell in their place. The destruction was complete or partial for some, that is, a small remnant of them remained according to the greatness of their evils; but God had commanded the destruction of all, yet the children of Israel were negligent in driving them out and killing them after Joshua.
Obedience to God's commandments protects you from the wars of the demons, so however hard they are, do not abandon them, but ask for His help that you may enjoy His care and love.

He also warns them against taking part in the worship of idols worshiped by the Gentiles in whose place they will dwell in the Promised Land, and moreover He asks them to tear down the walls and pillars and temples (their images) that they set up for their worship.
And if some object that killing these peoples involves cruelty, because they had no chance to know God, and what is the fault of their children who are killed, the answer to that is that:
1- God speaks to all human beings through His voice within them, which is the conscience.
2- Nature speaks of the existence of God and His oneness.
3- These peoples had heard of what God did with His people, their crossing of the Red Sea and the ten plagues, and this was enough for them to believe in Him.
4- There are examples of faith and life with God among the Gentiles, such as Rahab the harlot (Josh 2, 6:25) and Ruth.

5- The death of the children was painful to their fathers, that perhaps they might repent, and God, by His foreknowledge, knows that these children would have become wicked. Likewise God will judge the children who did not sin in a way different from the wicked adults.
He stresses to them that they should worship God only, and then God will bless their bread and their water and protect them from diseases and heal them from them if they afflict them.

God's blessing rests upon you if you worship Him and your heart does not cling to the material things of the world; He then provides for your material needs, and you are not hindered by illnesses or the obstacles of the world from worshiping Him, so you live in joy all your days until you reach the Kingdom.

God also promises them, if they hold fast to His worship, to bless every pregnant woman so that her child is not lost, and to give offspring from all the wombs of its women, so there is no barren one, that is, they increase in number and strength. Then He also promises them length of days, confirming the increase of their number.
All the people to whom thou shalt come: the pagan peoples whom you attack and drive out because of their evil.
Turn their backs: they run and flee before you.

God adds also that He appears in His majesty in His war with the enemies, so they fear and flee quickly from before the children of Israel. And the awe of God appears either in the dignity of His children, so that the enemies fear them, or by some other means such as the hornets (v. 28) or thunder.

Hornets: plural of hornet, an insect that gives unbearable stings, which God sends before the children of Israel in their war with the original inhabitants of the Promised Land, so they flee from before them in the war (Josh 24:12, Wis 12:8, 9).

Here appears God's wisdom in driving out the enemies gradually, so that there may be an opportunity for the children of Israel to build up the cities in their place. But if He drove them out quickly, the wild beasts would come and dwell in their abandoned cities and the children of Israel could not enter them; and at the same time, driving out the peoples gradually was an opportunity for these peoples to repent and for some of their individuals at least to return to God (Wis 12:10-27).

Do not be troubled if your striving against any sin lasts long, for God removes it from you gradually so that you do not fall into pride or any other sins, for He knows the fierceness of the devil, and at the same time you have an opportunity for your faith to be established through spiritual striving and to be strengthened by the grace of God.
Another reason for driving out the enemies gradually is to give the children of Israel an opportunity to take care of cultivating the land, so that they eat of its fruits and enjoy them.

God defined for him the area of the Promised Land that he would possess, which extends southward from the Red Sea (the Sea of Suph) to the northwest, which is the Mediterranean Sea, that is, the sea of the Philistines; and from the wilderness, that is, the wilderness of Sinai in the southwest, to the river, which is the river Euphrates in the northeast. This actually happened in the days of David and Solomon (1 Kgs 4:21, 24). But in the New Testament the people of God are those who believe in Christ in every place in the world, and not within the area of a particular land.

He requires him not to make peace or covenant with the inhabitants of the land and dwell with them, but to drive them out, lest if he mingles with them he becomes bound to the worship of idols and leaves God; and this actually happened in the era of the Judges (Judg 2, 3). But whoever of the pagan peoples believes joins the people of God, like Uriah the Hittite and Araunah the Jebusite (2 Sam 11:3, 24:16). The covenant with God and Moses' ascent of the mountain

entries.section: (1) The call of Moses to go up the mountain

paragraphs.text: Moses went up for the first time when God called him to receive the commandments and the Law (ch. 19). After he heard the Ten Commandments he went down to the people to tell them, and found them trembling at the sight of the smoking mountain (ch. 20:18-20); so he reassured them and went up to hear the ordinances of the Law mentioned in (ch. 21-23). And God calls him again to receive the pattern of the tabernacle of the congregation, and this time He calls with him Aaron and his two sons Nadab and Abihu and seventy of the elders of Israel, who are as their leaders and judges, and that is because he will receive the pattern of the tabernacle of the congregation, which will need the priestly work of Aaron and his sons.

And He asked them to worship afar off, at the foot of the mountain, because of the holiness of the mountain, since God had descended upon it in smoke, mist and fire, so that they might represent the people in submission to God, just as we now bow down in the church before the sanctuary, because Christ dwells in it with His Body and Blood.

Nadab and Abihu: the sons of Aaron, who came forward with their father and their uncle and saw, but who erred afterward by offering strange fire before God, and so died, although their position qualified them to advance in the priesthood and to cleave to God (Lev 10:1).

Seize the opportunity now to be joined to the Church and her sacraments, and if you have an opportunity to serve, do not leave it; and stand firm in humility before God in all His commandments and the teachings of the Church, for negligence was a cause of the destruction of many who were near to God, such as the priests Nadab and Abihu, and Judas Iscariot, the disciple of Christ.

entries.section: (1) The call of Moses to go up the mountain

paragraphs.text: This group leaves the people and draws near to the mountain, but the one who will go up the mountain and come near to God is Moses alone, because of his purity and holiness.
Moses told the assembled people what he had heard from God, both the Ten Commandments and the Law (ch. 20-23), and the people declared their submission and readiness to obey God's commands.

Moses wrote the Ten Commandments and the Law as much as he remembered by God's grace, and afterward he received the Ten Commandments written by God's hand on two tablets; and to express his thanks to God he built an altar below the mountain and twelve pillars around it representing the twelve tribes of the children of Israel, to declare that the salvation of all the people depends on the sacrifice offered, which signifies the crucified Christ.
Burnt offerings: sacrifices that are burned entirely on the altar to please God.

Peace offerings: sacrifices that are slaughtered and a part of them is offered on the altar, and the people eat of the rest. Moses commanded some young men to offer sacrifices of oxen to God in thanks for His commandments that He had given them, since the tribe of Levi had not yet been set apart for service nor Aaron for the priesthood.

Use your time in the days of your youth and in the time when you are able to offer God worship, for there may come times when your body weakens or the cares of life hinder you; and your store of spiritual work will remind you of God and bring you back to Him, so that you meditate on and repeat the word of God that you lived with Him earlier, and enjoy it all your days. And the days of youth are not only at a certain age but in every time in which you are able to work, whatever your age, as long as God has given you strength to work.

When the oxen were slaughtered, Moses commanded, and they gathered the blood in basins, that is, wide vessels, in which he put half of the blood; and the other half of the blood he sprinkled on the altar, declaring that this is the blood with which God is pleased with them, and it signifies the blood of Christ the Redeemer.
The book of the covenant: God's commandments and His law are a covenant between Him and His people; if they keep them, He blesses them in all their life.
Moses read the commandments and the Law that he had written in a book, and when the people heard the word of God they confirmed again their readiness to obey Him.

Moses sprinkled the blood that was in the basins on the people to sanctify them by it, for it is a type of the blood of Christ the Savior, which we receive today in the sacraments of the Church; and he calls it the blood of the covenant because it is a covenant between God and His people: if they obey His commandments, He will be their God and will keep them and save them from all evil.
Moses carried out the word of God mentioned in (vv. 1, 2) and went up on the mountain, and he and Aaron, Nadab, Abihu and the seventy elders drew near to the foot of the mountain.
As it were the body of heaven: like heaven itself.

When they drew near the mountain, God appeared upon it in a form that was perhaps the form of a man, and under His feet they saw something great that they could not define, so they said of it that it was "a likeness of a work", that is, something made by the hand of God; it resembles a cloud, but its color is light blue and pure like the transparent blue sapphire, which is one of the precious, costly stones, and its color was the color of the pure sky. It may have appeared as a great light or some awesome sight, with beneath it a work of sapphire. The meaning of this is that God made something of His glory and splendor appear, but of course they did not see God Himself, as He said, "No man shall see Me and live" (Ezek 33:20).
The nobles of the children of Israel: Aaron and his sons and the elders of the people.

And everyone who comes near the holy mountain dies, because of the greatness of God, but "He laid not His hand", that is, He did not harm the people when they drew near the mountain, because it was God who sanctified them and cared for them.

And they all rejoiced at seeing God, and to express their joy they sat down to eat of the food they had taken with them, which was the peace offerings that the young men offered by the hand of Moses (v. 5).

When you enjoy seeing God in your prayers and meditations, your life is turned into a blessing, and you are able to do everything in holiness, whether eating or drinking or sleeping or recreation, for all things are pure to the pure.

God commanded Moses to come forward and go up the mountain so that He might give him the Ten Commandments written on two tablets of stone, and also the Law that God Himself wrote. For although Moses wrote the commandments and the Law after he came down from the mountain, God writes them for him Himself, lest anything of them should have fallen from him by oversight.
The mount of God: this is Mount Sinai.

Moses went forward, going up the mountain, and Joshua, his special disciple, followed him; for Moses was careful to disciple others such as Joshua, and also the leaders, the elders of Israel, to lead the people, especially since Joshua needed special discipling because he would lead the people after Moses.

Take care to give everything you know to others and disciple them so that they too may give, and so on...; so do not be selfish but concerned to teach everyone, not only through yourself but also through those whom you have discipled.

As for the seventy elders, he said to them that it was enough for them to come near to the foot of the mountain and see God in the form of sapphire. And before he bade them farewell, he said to them that if a dispute arises among you in anything, return to Aaron and Hur, who was also a disciple of Moses and used to support his hand when he prayed so that they might overcome Amalek (ch. 17:12); he was the grandfather of Bezaleel, who led the workers in setting up and making the tabernacle of the congregation (ch. 35:30, 31), and some Bible scholars consider him to have been the husband of Miriam, the sister of Moses. And the seventy elders judge the children of Israel in their various cases.

Moses went forward with his disciple Joshua to go up the mountain, and here they saw the mountain covered with a cloud as a sign of the presence of God, because the cloud points to heaven, for God is exalted above our minds and thoughts. This cloud remained covering the mountain for six days, and whenever Moses and Joshua lifted their eyes they found a thick cloud covering the mountain. God left them for this period so that they might feel the fear of Him, and after six days God called Moses to enter into the midst of the cloud.
The top of the mountain appeared as if covered with fire above the cloud, also declaring the presence of God, who is a consuming fire that crushes all evil.
And all the people of Israel saw this wonderful sight from afar so that they might fear God and be sanctified.

Moses left Joshua his disciple in the middle of the mountain and went up toward the summit and disappeared in the midst of the cloud to meet God and remain with Him forty days, enjoying conversation with Him in them, learning from Him the pattern of the tabernacle of the congregation and receiving the tablets of the commandment and the Law; that is, this time he did not go up for a short period as in the previous times but remained 40 days. He went up again and remained another 40 days (Ex 34:28) to receive the tablets of the Law after the breaking of the first two tablets. His fasting was by divine help, because an ordinary person cannot endure fasting 40 days, and so Elijah also fasted by the help of God (1 Kgs 19:11); and these two were a type of the fasting of Christ for us forty days and forty nights (Mt 3). And as Moses fasted 40 days and received the word of God written on the tablets and the Law, so also Christ, after His fast of 40 days, delivered His Gospel on earth and then His death on the cross, that is, He is the Word of God who redeemed us that we might live by Him.

Gifts for the tent, the ark, the table and the lampstand. God gave Moses on the mountain the details of setting up the tabernacle of the congregation, and it was so called because God meets in it with His people (Josh 19:51). It was also called the tabernacle of the testimony (Num 9:15) because in it are the tablets of the commandments that bear witness to God in the midst of His people, and because the tent testifies that God is the God of this people and lives among them. It was also called the dwelling place because God dwells in the midst of His people (2 Sam 7:6), and likewise it was called the house of the LORD (Judg 19:18) since worship of Him is offered in it. It was also called the temple (1 Sam 1:9) because God dwells in it. It consists of the dwelling, which includes the Holy Place and the Holy of Holies, whose three walls are set up from wooden boards and covered with fabrics that become a roof for it and hang down on its sides and at its rear, while its door is made of a curtain, and a curtain also separates the Holy Place from the Holy of Holies. Inside the Holy of Holies is the ark of the covenant, which is the most important thing in the tent, and therefore He begins speaking of it in this chapter. And inside the Holy Place are three things: the table of the showbread, which is on the right of one entering the Holy Place, and in the middle the altar of incense, while on the left is the lampstand. Around the dwelling is the outer court, a courtyard surrounding the dwelling on all sides, and in front of the dwelling is the laver and before it the bronze altar.

The tent is surrounded by a fence made of wooden boards covered with curtains and fixed in the ground by bases and pegs. The door of the tent is on the eastern side and is a curtain hung on wooden boards, like the door of the Holy Place and the Holy of Holies, and when you pass through it and enter the outer court you find the bronze altar, followed by the laver, then the door of the Holy Place, and after it the door of the Holy of Holies, which is on the western side. Entering the Holy of Holies is permitted only to the high priest, once a year, on the Day of Atonement, while the Holy Place is entered only by the priests every day, and the outer court surrounding the Holy Place and the Holy of Holies, in which are the laver and the bronze altar, is permitted only to the Jews to enter, while non-Jews stand outside the tent.

The tabernacle of the congregation remained for 480 years. The first forty years were in the wilderness of Sinai, moving as God led the people by the pillar of cloud and the pillar of fire (Ex 40:36-38); then in the land of Canaan Joshua set it up at Gilgal (Josh 4:19) and then moved it to Shiloh (Josh 18:1), where it remained for 400 years. King Saul moved it to Nob (1 Sam 21:1-9), and after that David moved it to Gibeon (1 Chr 21:9, 2 Chr 1:3), and it continued there until Solomon built the temple in its place on a larger scale and probably put its furnishings in one of the side chambers (1 Kgs 6:1). And the grief of the people was great when the enemies took the ark of the covenant of God in the days of Samuel the prophet, and they remained in weakness until God brought it back in the days of David (2 Sam 6:17), who rejoiced in it greatly, he and all the people.

God commanded Moses to collect gifts from the people for the founding of the tabernacle of the congregation, so that each one might show the extent of his care for the love of God, and their gifts would increase in proportion to their love for Him. And these gifts they offered from what they had taken from the Egyptians when they left the land of Egypt.

God specified the kinds of gifts required, and this is what everyone who manages a project must do, specify what is required for it. He began with the required metals, which carry symbolic spiritual meanings, and they are:
1- Gold: it signifies faith in God.
2- Silver: it signifies the word of God.
3- Bronze: it signifies endurance.
He continues the required materials, asking for kinds of fabrics and their requisites:
4- Blue: a light blue fabric that signifies heaven.
5- Purple: a fabric of a red color tending to violet, which is the garment of kings and signifies the kingship of Christ.
6- Scarlet: a dark red fabric that signifies the blood of Christ.
7- Goats' hair: used in making fabrics and tents, and it signifies death to the world.
8- Fine linen: that is, flax used in making fabrics and worn by the priests, and it signifies purity.
9- Rams' skins dyed red: used in covering the tent and dyed red, and it signifies death to the world.

10- Badgers' skins: the badger (tahash) is a sea animal with a thick skin, and it includes the seal, the dolphin and the sea horse, and it is used as an outer covering for the tent because its color and shape are not beautiful, and it signifies death to the world.
11- Shittim wood: strong wood that does not decay, used in making the firm foundation, and it signifies purity and endurance.

These are the coverings of the tent and its pillars, which are made of wood; they represent the outer protection, so they must be strong (see figure 1). Coverings of badgers' skins; coverings of rams' skins dyed red; coverings of goats' skins, west; coverings of white linen (fine linen), north; the tabernacle of the congregation; south; the outer court; east; the door, the only entrance of the tent. Figure (1:) The tabernacle of the congregation (Ex 25-30)
He adds materials that are consumed during the service in the tabernacle of the congregation, which are:
12- Oil: for lighting the lampstand, and it is pure olive oil, and it signifies the Holy Spirit.

13- Spices: sweet scents that are added and from which the anointing oil is made, and it will be mentioned in detail in (ch. 30:21-38); with it the priests and kings and the tent and its contents are anointed, and it signifies the Holy Spirit, who gives off a sweet fragrance.
He adds materials for adornment, which are:

14- Precious stones: onyx stones or various kinds with which the breastplate of the high priest is adorned, and they signify the dignity of the priesthood and the greatness of every soul in the sight of God, for each stone signifies a tribe.

The breastplate: the high priest wore it on his chest (ch. 28:15-30). Sanctuary: where God dwells in the midst of His people, and it is called the tabernacle of the congregation because in it God meets with His people.

The love of God moves Him to dwell in the midst of His people because He wants to be joined to them, and that they gather around Him always and be sanctified, and the tabernacle of the congregation is to be a place for the sanctification of the people and their purification from all evil. And Moses makes this tent according to the pattern that God will show him on the mountain, which will be mentioned now after these verses, for the Church is the image of heaven on earth.
Take care that God has a place inside you and that you return to Him in all your affairs through prayer, and offer Him the best of your time and abilities so that you may enjoy His work in you.

An ark: it is also called the ark of the covenant, since in it are placed the two tablets of the Law, which are God's covenant with His people, and it is also called the ark of the testimony, since God testifies to Himself by these commandments before His people. The ark is placed in the Holy of Holies.

He began with the ark of the covenant, which points to the presence of God, for it is the most important thing in the tent. It is made of firm shittim wood that does not decay, as a type of purity and immortality. He gives its measurements in cubits, a cubit being about 50 cm, so its length is one and a quarter meters and its width 75 cm and its height 75 cm (figures 1, 2). Figure (2:) The ark of the covenant

The ark is overlaid with gold inside and out. Gold signifies divinity and heaven, for the splendor of divinity is within it and without it, and therefore he took care that the ark be overlaid on the inside although no one would see it. The crown around the ark signifies glory, and the purpose of making it is adornment and also to hold the cover in its place.
Thou shalt cast: you melt the gold and pour it into molds so that it has the required shape.

He also makes for the ark four feet, that is, four supports on each side on which the ark stands, and he makes on them four rings of gold, two on each side, for the staves to pass through by which the ark will be carried.

He also makes two staves of firm shittim wood and overlays them with gold and puts them in the rings, one on one side of the ark and the other on the other side, and they remain in them always so that the Levites may carry the ark by them when it is moved from one place to another during their journeying in the wilderness, because the ark is always covered and no one touches it because of its holiness, so the Levites carry it by the two staves only, and therefore the staves are never taken out of the ark. The two staves signify the priesthood, through whose help we are joined to God.
They dispensed with them in the temple of Solomon since there was no need to move the ark from place to place.

The most important thing placed in the ark is the tablets of the Law, that is, the tablets of the covenant written on two tablets of stone, and with them will also be placed the pot of manna and Aaron's rod (Heb 9:4), and the rod signifies divine care and the priesthood.

The tablets of the testimony: because by them God testifies to His people the word by which they ought to live, and having lived by it they testify by their lives to the whole world that they are the people of God.
Let the word of God be inside your heart and nothing else, for it is what moves your life and changes your conduct, so that your heart is not occupied with the cares or material things of the world.

The cover is the lid of the ark and is made of pure gold, and it is called the mercy seat or the throne, and it signifies the mercy of God, since blood is sprinkled on it every year and divine justice, represented by the cherubim, sees it and pardons human beings; and this blood is a reference to the blood of Christ. It is the size of the ark, that is, its length is one and a quarter meters and its width 75 cm. It is placed on the ark and the crown surrounding the ark bounds it and encircles it on all sides, so that the cover does not move; the crown works as a barrier that keeps the cover in its place so that it does not fall from above the ark. The cover is made of pure gold because it signifies Christ, who covered us and made atonement for us by His blood, and it also signifies the Virgin, over whom the angels overshadow because Christ is in her womb.
Of beaten work: casting.

He asked him to make two angels of the rank of the cherubim, that is, the Cherubim, which signify divine justice. They are all made of gold, one piece with the cover, the head of each one facing the other and looking toward the cover, and each angel stretches his wings toward the other so that they meet at their tips. The form of the angel is probably the form of a man, and they look toward the cover, toward the blood that will be sprinkled upon it, so that when divine justice sees the blood, which points to the blood of Christ, that is, divine mercy, it pardons man. And the wings are raised on high to declare that they are from heaven.
And the cherubim are a great angelic rank that signifies abundant knowledge, since they are full of eyes, and they represent:
1- The presence of God.
2- Divine justice, when they were placed at the gate of the garden of Eden to prevent man's return (Gen 3:24).
3- The praise of God.

God declared that He would speak with His people from above the cover, because the ark signifies Christ, the wood His body and the gold His divinity. And God will speak from between the angels, which signify His justice, and at the same time from above the mercy seat on which the blood is sprinkled, so His justice will be mingled with His mercy when He speaks with the people.
And from the foregoing we see that the ark and the cover signify Christ in the following:
1- The presence of God in the midst of His people.
2- The wood signifies the humanity and the gold the divinity, so the ark signifies Christ, God incarnate.
3- The ark contains the tablets of the Law, that is, the word of God, and Christ is the Word of God.
4- The ark contains the pot of manna, and Christ is the manna come down from heaven to give Himself as food for His people, that is, His most holy Body and Blood.
5- The ark contains Aaron's rod that budded, which signifies the incarnate Christ, who gave us life from death.

6- And the cover on which the blood is sprinkled signifies Christ, who paid our debts with His blood before divine justice. And all these types, that is, the ark and what is in it and on it, also signify the Virgin Mary, as appears from the Sunday Theotokia.
Seize the opportunity of your life to enjoy God's mercy through your repentance and return to Him, and so escape the punishment of His justice.

This table is also made of firm shittim wood and is placed on the right as the priest enters the Holy Place; its length is two cubits, about one meter, its width one cubit, about 50 cm, and its height a cubit and a half, about 75 cm (figure 3). Figure (3:) The table of the showbread
It is also overlaid with gold, and a crown is made for it that surrounds it and keeps the bread from falling off it.

The border is a belt that ties the legs together and fixes them, and it is below the surface of the table for placing the vessels on it. This border has a crown, that is, a lip that holds the vessels on it so that they do not fall, and it is a handbreadth below the surface of the table, that is, a handbreadth wide, and this handbreadth is probably equal to the grasp of the hand, about 10 cm, and it extends outside it by a handbreadth also.

Four rings are made on the border, which is the outer perimeter of the table, and two staves of shittim wood overlaid with gold are made and put in the rings for carrying the table during the journeying in the wilderness, a reference to the sojourn of the world.

He mentions the vessels used for the service of the table, which are: The dishes: plates by which the bread is carried to the table. The spoons: small dishes in which incense is placed. The covers and bowls: in which wine is placed.
And all these utensils are made of pure gold.

12 loaves are placed, the number of the twelve tribes of the children of Israel, in two rows on the table, six loaves in each row, for a week, and then they are changed and others put in their place, and the old ones are eaten only by the priests, and they signify Christ our satisfaction and the special grace given to the priests. It is called the showbread because it is placed before the face of God, so there is a special blessing in it. Frankincense and salt were placed on it, and the frankincense signifies the priesthood of Christ and the salt the covenant He made with us by our redemption on the cross, that we might live for Him.
May you take care to be nourished by the word of God and that your heart be open before Him in much prayer, and so receive His blessing.

The lampstand consists of three parts: a base, a shaft and six branches, and it is made from one block of gold that is beaten until it takes the shape of this lampstand, because the Holy Spirit is one essence that is not divided. The lampstand is placed on the left as the priest enters the Holy Place, and it is the only source of light inside it (figure 4). Figure (4:) The golden lampstand
The lampstand has seven branches: the upright shaft and three branches from each side of the shaft. And the number seven signifies the Holy Spirit, who works in the seven sacraments of the Church.

On each branch is a cup like the cup of a flower, and under it a knop, that is, a knot or a pomegranate. And there is a cup at the top of the branch with a flower inside it, that is, like the green leaves that have within them and at their top the colored petals of the flower. There are three cups on the branch, each cup with a pomegranate under it, so the three cups are in succession, one at the first third, the second at the top of the second third and the third at the top of the branch, which is where the oil and the lamps are.

This ornament was made on every branch, pomegranates and cups and flowers, to declare that God is the source of life for His people. And this life appears in the flowers and fruits of plants, that is, the cups, the flowers and the pomegranates. And the number three signifies the Holy Trinity.

The middle shaft between the six branches has along its length four cups with their flowers: the first at the top of the first quarter, the second at the top of the middle, the third at the top of the three quarters and the fourth at the top of the shaft. And the number four signifies the four corners of the inhabited world, that is, the Holy Spirit is one of the three hypostases who enlightens the whole world with its four corners. For God in His three hypostases is the source of light and life for every person.

Under every two branches where they come out of the shaft is a knop, that is, a small pomegranate; that is, at the going out of the branches there are three pomegranates, and from each pomegranate two branches come out. Thus the work of lighting is blended with the life that the pomegranate signifies, because the pomegranate is the fruit of a living plant, for the Holy Spirit is the source of light and life for every person.

The lampstand is made, as we mentioned, from one block of pure gold, because the Holy Spirit is the source of purity for the whole world. And gold signifies divinity and heaven, the dwelling of God, who gives us the Holy Spirit.

He places the lamps at the edge of each cup, that is, the wicks face toward the middle shaft, so that their light is more concentrated; this is what he calls "give light over against it", that is, the manifold work of the Holy Spirit in the form of the seven sacraments has one purpose that is gathered in the salvation of man and his union with God.
The tongs: similar to the tongs known now, used for adjusting the wicks and putting them in or lifting them.
A talent: equal to 44 kg of gold.

The snuffdishes: vessels like an ashtray now, small dishes in which the new wicks or those that have been used are placed (figure 4). The whole lampstand and its utensils are made of pure gold, which signifies the purity of the work of the Holy Spirit, and are made of the same one block as we mentioned, whose amount is a talent.
All these details Moses saw on the mountain as God showed them to him.

God is the source of enlightenment and guidance in every aspect of your life through His many-sided work. So ask for His guidance and submit to Him even if it conflicts with your mind or your emotions.
The coverings of the tent and its pillars
Curtain: a rectangular piece of cloth.
Fine twined linen: linen made of threads twisted together to form a multi-stranded thread, from which this piece of cloth is woven.
Weaver: tailor.
Skilled: expert.

1- The first covering that a person sees on entering the Holy Place or the Holy of Holies is made of linen, embroidered with cloth of blue, purple and scarlet. The linen signifies purity, the blue signifies heaven, the purple signifies kingship, and the scarlet signifies redemption and blood (figs. 5, 6).
2- The number 10 signifies the commandments, for the word of God is the basis of the relationship between man and God, so that He may meet with him.
3- A picture of angels of the order of the Cherubim is embroidered on the curtain in order to proclaim:
a- The presence of God and heaven.
b- The justice of God, which is satisfied when it sees the blood of the sacrifices, which signifies the blood of Christ.
c- To encourage us to join the angels in praising God.

The joined set. The joined set. 50 loops on each side. 10 cubits (the roof). 9 cubits. 9 cubits (the north side) (the south side). A cubit. The colored curtains. 5 curtains, their length 20 cubits. Two loops through which a gold clasp passes. Folded curtains. The entrance. Goats' hair curtains cover the colored curtains. The colored curtains cover the whole tabernacle from below and hang down from them at the back, and do not hang down from them. They touch the boards, and the curtains. A part. Something. And a cubit rises from the ground, of goats' hair, on the outside. And the clasps above one another.
Figure (5:) The curtains of the linen covering and the goats' hair covering

The curtain: a rectangular piece of cloth made of linen, 28 cubits long, which is the product of (7 x 4), that is, the work of the Holy Spirit, signified by the number (7), in the whole world, signified by the number (4). The width of the curtain is (4) cubits, which signifies the world with its four corners, so the curtain proclaims the work of God in the world. All the curtains are equal in length and width.
Coupled: sewn with ordinary sewing.
Every five curtains are sewn together, so that in the end we have two large pieces of cloth, each measuring 28 x 20 cubits.
Loops: the plural of a loop, which is a small opening in the cloth made with blue thread, that is, of a blue color.
Edge: the end of the curtain, 28 cubits long.
The coupling: the piece of cloth in which five curtains are joined.
Loops are made on the edge of the coupling along the 28 cubits.

Fifty loops are made on the edge of each coupling, opposite one another, and the distance between one loop and the next is about 28 cm. The number 50 signifies the Holy Spirit who descended on the day of Pentecost. The two large curtains signify the Gentiles and the Jews, and what binds them together is the Holy Spirit, who leads them to faith in Christ.
Clasps: the plural of a clasp, which is a metal alloy that can be bent like wire.

Fifty gold clasps are made, each one to join two loops together, and they are made of gold, which signifies heaven and divinity, so that whoever enters the Holy Place and the Holy of Holies may sense the presence of God.

Thus the two large pieces of cloth, each measuring 28 cubits x 20 cubits, are joined together by means of the loops and clasps and become a single piece of cloth measuring 28 cubits x 40 cubits. In practical terms, the covering was made of two pieces joined by clasps so that each piece could be carried separately when moving camp.

The number 40 signifies the Ten Commandments carried out in the whole world with its four corners (10 x 4). The large piece of cloth measuring 28 x 40 is placed so that the side 28 long runs from north to south, that is, it covers the roof, which is 10 cubits, and hangs down 9 cubits on each of the two sides, while the side 40 cubits long runs from east to west, 30 cubits of it covering the roof and 10 cubits hanging down at the back of the tabernacle, that is, representing the west wall of the Holy of Holies, so that the west side is covered down to the ground, while the north and south sides are a cubit above the ground on each side.

The tent of meeting proclaims from within that it is heaven, and it shows the justice of God in the Cherubim, so as to impart the fear of God to those who enter. You too, in the Church, may you sense the presence of God and the fear of Him, in addition to His love, which sends angels to you to help you in your striving.

The second covering is made of goats' hair and is made like the first covering, from a set of curtains, but their number here is (11) curtains instead of (10) curtains (figs. 5, 6). Figure (6:) The coverings of the tent

It is noted here that the size of the curtains made of goats' hair is longer than the linen curtains mentioned before, for the size of each curtain is (30 x 4) cubits. This is so that it covers the tent on its north and south sides and reaches the ground, and whoever enters the tent sees the linen covering and one cubit at the bottom, next to the ground, of the goats' hair covering.

Five curtains of goats' hair are sewn together, so that their size is (20 x 30) cubits, which equals (5 x 4 x 30) cubits, while the other six curtains are sewn together to become one piece called the coupling, whose size is (6 x 4 x 30) cubits, that is, (24 x 30) cubits.

These two couplings are joined together with loops and clasps as in the linen covering mentioned before, and they form the second covering of the tent, which is placed over the linen covering, so that its total length is 44 x 30 cubits. The thirty cubits cover the roof and the two sides, on the north and south, while the length of 44 covers the roof and the back of the tent, that is, the west side. As for the door of the Holy Place, one curtain 4 cubits long hangs down over it from above, and six cubits from the ground up to the curtain remain without a covering of goats' hair.
Fifty loops are made on the edge of each coupling, opposite the other, in the second covering made of goats' hair.

The clasps here are made of bronze, which signifies earnestness and spiritual striving, or steadfastness in striving. They join the fifty loops, and the distance between one loop and the next is about 30 cm, and thus the two pieces of cloth are joined to form a covering 44 x 30 cubits long. It is noted that the joining of the two couplings will be above and around the veil that separates the Holy Place from the Holy of Holies.
The overhanging part is half of the curtain, that is, half of the coupling, one part of which is on the roof, while the other part hangs down on the west side.

The coupling, which is also called the curtain and includes 5 curtains, will cover the Holy of Holies, which is ten cubits, and then it hangs down at the back of the house, that is, the west side, to a height of ten cubits.

It is noted that the second covering, of goats' hair, has a width of (30) cubits, that is, two cubits longer than the linen covering, so it covers one cubit more than the linen covering on each side and reaches the ground on the north and south sides.

The third covering of the tent, which is placed over the two previous coverings, is made of rams' skins, tanned or dyed red, as a reference to the blood of Christ. It is a stronger and poorer covering, that is, not precious like the previous coverings. It protects the previous coverings and the tent from rain and dust. Then a fourth, thick covering, stronger than the third, is placed on it, made of badgers' skins, which is poorer than the three previous coverings and stronger, to protect them from rain and wind. No measurements are mentioned for the third and fourth coverings, but it is implicitly understood that they are longer than the previous coverings in order to cover them completely, especially the fourth covering, because the thick covering may be somewhat domed over the roof, which helps the rainwater run down on both sides of the tabernacle (figs. 1, 6). It is noted that the tent is very precious in its coverings on the inside but poorer in its outer coverings, which people see, like Christ, who is God, and in whom are all the treasures of knowledge, wisdom and love, but from the outside is a suffering and crucified man. After His likeness is the Christian, in whom the Holy Spirit comforts him and gladdens him, but on the outside he is suffering and persecuted by the world.
Seek the virtues of others that are hidden within them, and do not judge by appearance, so that you may discover God dwelling in them.

The tabernacle: it is so called because God dwells in it in the midst of His people; it is also called the tent of meeting because He meets with His people in it; it is also called the tent of the testimony because in it are the two tablets of the testimony, that is, the Ten Commandments, which are the words of God that bear witness to Him; and it is also called the house of the Lord because He dwells in it.

Wooden boards are made for the tabernacle, that is, for the Holy of Holies and the Holy Place, representing the north, west and south walls of the Holy Place and the Holy of Holies. They are made of acacia wood, which is durable wood that woodworms do not attack, that is, it lasts a long time without decay, as a reference to the pure and holy humanity of Christ (figs. 7, 8). 10 cubits. 6 boards. The double board. Two tenons joined to one another. Figure (7) The boards of the tabernacle. The double board. The double board. 6 boards. The north wall (20 boards). The south wall (20 boards). 20 boards. The width of the board is 1.5 cubits. Each board has 3 rings through which the bars pass. Two tenons joined. The hangings. 5 pillars to carry one another. The curtain of the entrance. Figure (8) The boards of the tabernacle

Each board is 10 cubits long, that is, the height of the Holy Place or the Holy of Holies from the ground to the roof is 10 cubits, while the width of the board is a cubit and a half, but its thickness is not mentioned.
Two tenons are made for each board, fixed in it or in one piece with it. This board could be several boards fastened completely together to form one board.

The number of boards toward the south, that is, the right, is twenty boards, and each board is a cubit and a half wide, so the total width of the boards, if they are set close together, is 30 cubits, which is the length of the Holy Place and the Holy of Holies. It is understood from this that the south wall is a complete wooden wall 10 cubits high and 30 cubits long.

Each tenon of the board is placed in a silver base, which represents the foundation for the two tenons of the board, or for the whole tabernacle. And since we have 20 boards, we need 40 bases, which are dug into the ground and into which the tenons of the boards are fitted, so that the wooden wall is fixed in the ground by means of the silver bases. Silver signifies the word of God, for the foundation of the relationship with God is attachment to His word, and Christ, the Word of God, is the foundation of salvation, and the two tenons of each board signify the Jews and the Gentiles, or the Old and New Testaments.

The north wall of the tabernacle is exactly like the south wall, consisting of twenty boards ten cubits high, with 40 tenons fixed in 40 bases. The boards are set close together and form a wall 30 cubits long.
"Alike they shall be coupled at the top": that is, its thickness is double the thickness of the ordinary board from its bottom to its top.
