2- That He not give the Gentiles, such as the Egyptians, an opportunity to speak arrogantly against God and claim that He hates His people and brought them out with cunning in order to destroy them in the wilderness, whereas God is tender and compassionate and does not lie in His promises. That is, that He not give them an opportunity to gloat over His people.

3- He reminds God of His promises to the fathers, Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, to give them the land of Canaan. Here the unselfishness of Moses appears: he does not think of himself and his house becoming the beginning of the people of God as Abraham did, but with fatherly love he cares for the salvation of all the people, even though they are wicked. Moses reminds God that the people are His people, so that He may have mercy on them.

The Lord repented: He turned back from His decision. It does not mean that He felt He had made a mistake, because God knows everything and does not err, but He speaks in the manner that human beings understand, namely that He is a tender Father who gave up His decision to destroy the people, agreed to Moses' intercession for his people, and abandoned His decision to destroy them. He knows what will happen and that Moses will intercede for them, but He wanted to declare what they deserve, and then, for the sake of Moses' intercession, to have mercy on them.

entries.section: (3) The anger of Moses and the breaking of the tablets

paragraphs.text: On both their sides: on both faces.

Moses obeyed and went down from the mountain, departing from the presence of God, whom he saw in a certain form that may have been light or some other dazzling and wonderful form. In his hands were the two tablets of stone that God had given him, with the Ten Commandments written on both sides of each tablet. The two tablets were made by God and written by Him, and Moses alone carried them in his hands, rejoicing in their great value.

entries.section: (3) The anger of Moses and the breaking of the tablets

paragraphs.text: After Moses had descended some distance on the mountain, he met his disciple Joshua, who had been waiting for him for the forty days. He rejoiced at meeting him, and they went down together. When they drew near the foot of the mountain, before they saw the people, they heard the sound of their shouting, and Joshua thought it was the sound of battle, perhaps the people fighting the Amalekites, who had risen against them a second time.

entries.section: (3) The anger of Moses and the breaking of the tablets

paragraphs.text: Being overcome: defeat.
Moses answered Joshua, denying his words and declaring that these sounds were not the sounds of battle, whether the voice of the victors or of the defeated, but the sound of the people singing.

entries.section: (3) The anger of Moses and the breaking of the tablets

paragraphs.text: Moses and Joshua continued descending from the mountain and drew near to the people, and Moses saw the golden calf raised up and the people around it dancing and singing. He became very angry at the corruption of his people in leaving God and worshiping idols, and in the intensity of his anger he cast the two tablets from him despite their great value. But he was jealous with the jealousy of a father who cares for his children when he saw them in this corruption and turning away from God.

entries.section: (3) The anger of Moses and the breaking of the tablets

paragraphs.text: When the people saw Moses coming quickly toward them, they were very afraid. He took the calf and threw it into the fire until it melted and became a shapeless mass, then he broke it and ground it into tiny particles and cast them into the water, and the particles floated on the surface of the water. He commanded the people to drink of it, to show them the weakness of what they had imagined to be a god, so that they would feel their sin against God when they drank, that perhaps they might repent.

Be firm with those who err, if you are responsible for your household or your work or a group of those you serve in the Church. Reject evil and remove it from the midst, keep those you serve away from it, and make them know the extent of their sin so that they may repent. But your firmness should be with fatherhood and embrace toward those you rebuke, so that they do not fall into despair or obstinacy.
Moses rebuked Aaron for yielding to the evil thoughts of the people by making a calf and calling them to worship it. By this he made them idolaters, and they disobeyed God and defied Him.
Aaron did not admit his fault but gave justifications for what he had done, which are:
(1) That the people fall into many evils, such as murmuring, as Moses knows.
(2) Moses represented the image of God to the people, so when he was absent on the mountain for a long time, they asked for a tangible image to worship.

(3) He lessened his sin by saying that he was compelled to ask them for the gold earrings and throw them into the fire, and so a calf came out, although in truth he had made an effort and used the graving tool and instruments to make a calf of gold; it did not become a calf by itself.

We notice that Aaron called Moses "my lord" although he was younger than he, out of respect for him because he was the leader of the people and the prophet of God. This speech shows the seriousness of the leader's sin, which brings punishment upon all his people, for Aaron's laxity and his yielding to the evil of his people made the people fall into the sin of idolatry.

Moses grieved when he saw a large number of the people stripped of their clothes, even if partially, and immersed in the shamelessness or licentiousness and dancing that Aaron had allowed as leader of the people, so they became a derision among their neighbors, such as the Amalekites.

Bear your responsibility, whether you are a servant, or the head of a family, or someone responsible in any place, to lead others in the way of God, and do not abandon them or encourage them in evil. For God will hold you accountable because you used your leadership and your position to keep people away from God.
The gate of the camp: the entrance to the place where they pitched their tents; perhaps they posted guards at it against an attack by the Amalekites or any of their enemies.
Who is on the Lord's side: whoever believes in God and fears Him and rejects evil.
Let him come to me: let him come toward me to help me destroy evil.

Moses stood in a visible place, which was the entrance of the place where they were dwelling, and called to the people that everyone who fears God and is zealous to please Him should gather around him. A large number of the men of the tribe of Levi, who cared for their spiritual life and their relationship with God, gathered with him.

When Moses declared the wrath of God over their worship of the calf, and had ground it, scattered it on the water and made them drink of it, many were ashamed and repented and went into their tents, but some neglected the words of Moses and persisted in their evil. Then he commanded the sons of Levi gathered around him that each one take his sword, which was placed in a sheath at the middle of each man and hung on his thigh, and pass through the tents and kill their brothers who persisted in the games of shamelessness and dancing and had stripped off their clothes. The sons of Levi obeyed the word of Moses at once and killed three thousand men of the wicked.
Consecrate yourselves (literally, fill your hands): sanctify and set apart your works for God.
Every man on his son and on his brother: by killing the wicked son or brother.

After the destruction of the evil, Moses encouraged them, saying that by this they had obeyed God and sanctified their works by destroying the wicked, even if they were their sons or their brothers, for their relationship with God is more important than emotional relationships, and by this God gives them a great blessing. Filling the hand was an expression used in the priestly work when they carry the sacrifices on their hands and offer them on the altar before God. So he called the tribe of Levi, which would be set apart for the service of God, and from which would come Aaron and his sons, to destroy the wicked, because by destroying evil they would be doing work like the priests who sanctify God, whether by offering sacrifices or by the various purifications. Here, by their destroying evil, they declare the holiness of God, who is not in agreement with evil, and please Him, and by destroying the wicked they also save the people from the spread of evil among them, so that the fear of God falls on all hearts.

On the day after the killing of the wicked, Moses showed his people how monstrous their sin was and that they deserved severe punishment, but he gave them hope that he would go up to the mountain and pray to God to ask forgiveness for their sin. This shows that many had sinned and bowed down to the calf, but they repented at Moses' call and went into their tents, and the Levites did not kill them.

Moses confessed the sin of his people before God when he returned and went up to the mountain, where he had been with God forty days. Then he interceded for them that God might forgive them, and offered himself as a ransom for his people, that he should die but the people live. Here the fatherhood of Moses appears and his readiness to lay down his life for his people as a good shepherd to them, after the pattern of Christ the Redeemer. The blotting out of his name from the book of God means his death, or not being mentioned in the Holy Bible as one of the pious. Moses was not able to redeem his people, because only Christ is able to die for His people and make atonement for them, but by these words he shows his intense love and fatherhood for his wicked people.

Pray for those around you and care for the salvation of their souls. Rather, be ready to sacrifice anything material and to bear many hardships in order to win them for Christ, remembering your Redeemer who laid down His life for you.

God rejoiced in the fatherly feelings of Moses for his people, but He showed His justice by declaring that the one who sinned is the one who bears the punishment, and if he repents God accepts him. It is not right that one person die for another, because of man's weakness and because Christ alone is able to do this in the fullness of time.
Lead the people: exhort them so that they do not return to evil and so that they repent of their sin.
The day of My visitation: the day that God appoints to punish and discipline His people so that they feel the monstrousness of their sins and keep away from them.

God asked Moses to go down from the mountain and exhort the people to an upright life. He promised him that His angel would not leave them because of their sin, but would continue to lead them in the form of the pillar of cloud and the pillar of fire by day and by night, but that He would discipline them at the proper time so that they would not return to their sins. This means God's anger against them, so He deprived them of His presence in their midst and was content with the angel going before them.

God disciplined the people with plagues so that they would feel the monstrousness of idolatry. The kind of plagues is not mentioned, whether they were diseases or hunger or any other afflictions that God allowed for them, but what is mentioned is the death of three thousand of them in one day by the hand of their brothers (v. 28). Notice that His acceptance of Moses' intercession does not mean the complete removal of punishment from them but its lessening, whereas the complete removal of punishment is what is accomplished by the blood of Christ. This confirms the seriousness of sin and its consequences, which deserve many punishments, and so the love of Christ appears, which removes from us all these punishments.
God's leading of His people

Although the people of God fell into the worship of idols and departed from God, He did not reject them but remained faithful to His promises despite their unfaithfulness. So He spoke to Moses that he might prepare to enter the Promised Land, as God had promised the fathers Abraham, Isaac and Jacob.

Be steadfast in your love for those around you, even if they wrong you or do not respond to your love... Make excuses for them, and know that the continuance of your love and care for them establishes you in love and gradually affects them, and qualifies you to receive many divine blessings, the first of which is that you enjoy a strong experience of the love of God and His work in your life.
God promised to bring them into the Promised Land, but their leader would be an angel whom God would send, and not God Himself, because of His anger against them on account of their worship of idols.

Flowing with milk and honey: an expression for the many good things they will find in the Promised Land. The reason God would not lead them Himself on their way to the Promised Land, which is full of good things, is that they are quick to disobey and rebel, so they deserve the wrath of God and are exposed to destruction, that is, God would destroy them as a punishment for them.

The people felt their sin when they heard from Moses that God refused to lead them, and they wept in repentance before God, declaring their sin and asking forgiveness from Him. They stripped off their ornaments as a declaration of their clinging to God and their rejection of anything material for His sake.
Horeb: the place where they made the golden calf.

God affirmed the obstinacy of the people, signified by the stiffness of the neck, as animals are stubborn and turn and twist their necks, refusing to bear the yoke, that is, the wood that is placed on their necks to pull the agricultural implements. Therefore God withdrew from leading them Himself, yet in His tenderness He gave them an opportunity to repent by saying, "put off your ornaments," that is, repent and humble yourselves before Me, and I will consider what to do with you. So they hastened to repentance, humility and prayer, and put off their ornaments. Putting off ornaments was a well-known practice used in the East as a sign of mourning.

(2) God speaks in the tabernacle (v. 7: 11:) 7 And Moses took the tabernacle, and pitched it without the camp, afar off from the camp, and called it the Tabernacle of the congregation. And it came to pass, that every one which sought the LORD went out unto the tabernacle of the congregation, which was without the camp. 8 And it came to pass, when Moses went out unto the tabernacle, that all the people rose up, and stood every man at his tent door, and looked after Moses, until he was gone into the tabernacle. 9 And it came to pass, as Moses entered into the tabernacle, the cloudy pillar descended, and stood at the door of the tabernacle, and the LORD talked with Moses. 10 And all the people saw the cloudy pillar stand at the tabernacle door: and all the people rose up and worshipped, every man in his tent door. 11 And the LORD spake unto Moses face to face, as a man speaketh unto his friend. And he turned again into the camp: but his servant Joshua, the son of Nun, a young man, departed not out of the tabernacle.

Moses had a tent in which he met with the elders of Israel and judged the people, and this was different from the tent in which he lived with his family. He moved this tent outside the camp, that is, the place where the children of Israel pitched their tents, as a declaration of God's wrath, which was still upon His people, until they completed their repentance. Everyone of the people who had a request before God would go out to this tent and ask Moses to pray for him and would seek God in this place. This shows the mercy of God, who did not forsake them completely but only showed His displeasure with them so that they would repent.

This tent is a symbol of the Church, because in it God meets with His people, so it was called the tabernacle of meeting. It is a prelude to the tabernacle of meeting and of the testimony, in which is the Ark of the Covenant, the pattern of which Moses saw on the mountain because it had not yet been made (chs. 25-27).

Every need you feel, present it to God in the Church, place it on the altar. For when God sees your faith and your clinging to Him and your hastening to Him, and not to reason, the world and people, He has compassion on you, solves all your problems and blesses your life.

When Moses went out from his tent, in which he lived with his family, and passed through the tents of Israel on his way to the tabernacle of meeting outside the camp, everyone would come out of his tent and stand in respect for him and ask for prayer for himself and his family, and they would remain standing in reverence until he reached the tabernacle of meeting and entered it to meet with God.

God would declare His presence and His being with Moses, when he entered the tabernacle of meeting, by the pillar of cloud descending, covering, and standing before the door of the tabernacle until God's talk with Moses was finished. Moses would hear Him clearly and speak with Him, and then report to the people God's commands and commandments. Therefore he was called the one to whom God spoke, because of the abundance of His speaking with him. Because of his righteousness he reached the degree of direct conversation with God. By this he was able to lead the people with God's guidance, so that every servant and every head of a family may learn that prayer is the foundation of his success in leading those he serves and cares for.
When the people saw God appearing in the pillar of cloud, they would fear and bow down at once, each one before the door of his tent, in reverence and humility, asking for the mercies of God.

A wonderful friendship of the highest level was enjoyed by Moses with God through his successive meetings with Him in the tabernacle. His servant and disciple Joshua the son of Nun accompanied him and stood at the door of the tabernacle, and when Moses finished speaking with God and went to the people to teach them, Joshua would remain in the tabernacle in continual prayers and worship. Thus we see how God prepared Joshua through his discipleship to Moses and his learning worship for long periods, as he left his family and stayed in the tabernacle until the tabernacle of the testimony was made, in which is the Ark, and the Levites became responsible for guarding it and being present in it. Notice that this temporary tent was outside the camp as a declaration of God's wrath, but after they offered repentance, Moses set up the permanent tabernacle of meeting in the midst of the camp.

entries.section: (3) Moses' intercession that God might lead His people

paragraphs.text: Moses appealed to God and said to Him, You commanded me to bring up this people and take them to the land of Canaan, and You did not tell me whom You will send with me, meaning that You refused to lead the people Yourself, as You Yourself brought us out of the land of Egypt into the wilderness. He pleaded with Him to lead them and bear with them and not send with them only an angel, and he based his appeal on the following:
(1) God said, You have declared that You know me by name, that is, that You have loved me.

(2) In humility Moses declared his ignorance in leading the people and his need of God to make the way known to him. (3) Moses showed his longing to know God, as though he did not yet know Him, although he had a long fellowship with Him; he is ambitious to know God every day more than before.
(4) He reminds God that the children of Israel are His own people, for whom He is responsible, for He is their Father, their Shepherd and their God.

God is very tender, so ask of Him all that you want, and whatever your sins may be, know that He is ready to forgive you, and even if He is angry with you, continue in your supplication and humility before Him until you obtain His mercies.

entries.section: (3) Moses' intercession that God might lead His people

paragraphs.text: God agreed, before the appeal of Moses, to go Himself in the midst of His people and lead them. Moses affirmed that he would not move with this people except under the leadership of God, for remaining in the wilderness with God is better than entering the Promised Land with all its good things without God, because he loved God above all the material things of the world and found in Him his rest and reassurance.

entries.section: (3) Moses' intercession that God might lead His people

paragraphs.text: Moses continues his talk with God, declaring that the reason for his distinction and that of his people from all the peoples of the earth is the presence of God in their midst. He is the most precious thing in his life and the life of his people, and by this this people declare their faith in God to the whole world, so that they may believe and join the people of God and find their salvation. In the face of Moses' love and clinging to God, God affirmed to him that He would go before him and would not leave them, because He loved Moses and found in him righteousness and holiness.
Moses made a wonderful request that no one had made before, namely to see God. Although he had spoken with Him much, his longing for God led him to make this request.
I will make all My goodness pass before you: I will present My mercies before you, and My blessings and My good things.

I will proclaim the name of the LORD before you: I will declare Myself before you so that you may believe in Me and live with Me, you and your people. I will be gracious to whom I will be gracious, and will show mercy on whom I will show mercy: I give My love to whom I choose, and he is the one who believes in Me and responds to Me, and I pour out mercies upon him.

God said to him, I will give you many blessings and declare My name before you and have mercy on you, so you will see Me through these blessings and declarations and mercies, and this is quite enough.

God said to Moses, I love you and you have found grace in My sight, but this request of yours is beyond your endurance, for no man can see Me, meaning the seeing of the essence of God, because he would die from the greatness of the light of God and His brightness, which exceeds the capacities of human beings. For the angels, who are great creatures, cannot look at God but hide their faces from the brightness of His glory (Isa 6:2).

The tenderness of God could not bear, before the request of Moses and his insistence, to deprive His son of seeing Him, so He let him see Him to the extent that he could bear. God took Moses upon a rock and put him in a cleft and covered him with His hand, and then God passed by in His glory, that is, a great dazzling light appeared. Then God lifted His hand, and Moses saw something of the brightness of God, which is what he could bear as a man. He rejoiced greatly, and indeed his face was clothed with intense radiance, so that the children of Israel afterward could not bear to look at him and asked him to put a veil over his face (ch. 34:34, 35). Moses' seeing of God signifies the Incarnation of Christ. When God said, "Behold, there is a place by me," He meant the fullness of time when Christ became incarnate in Bethlehem, and the rock signifies Christ, upon whom the believer stands and sees God, and He reveals to him as much as he can bear. This is what we behold in the New Testament at Communion from the Holy Mysteries, and as God reveals Himself to His saints in the wildernesses throughout the ages. All this we behold now on earth, but in heaven we shall be able to see Him more clearly. Here we see Him as in a mirror, but there face to face, where our earthly bodies are changed and become spiritual bodies able to enjoy the sight of God clearly (1 Cor 13:10-12).

God loves you and wants to reveal His secrets to you if you want Him and seek Him. This appears in your striving toward prayer, reading and meditation, for in proportion to your care God will let you experience Him and rejoice in Him. The renewal of the covenant

God asked Moses to cut two tablets so that God might write on them the Ten Commandments. So he cut the two tablets in a reasonable size that could be carried and also afterward placed in the Ark of the Covenant. Notice that the two tablets the first time were made by the hand of God, but the second time Moses made them, so that God might show them the result of their sin in worshiping the golden calf, which angered Moses so that he broke the tablets.
Do not be careless in seizing every spiritual opportunity to draw near to God and to thank Him for His gifts, lest these blessings be lost to you and you not find them even if you seek them much.

He commanded him to rise early in the morning and go up with the tablets on the mountain to its top, that is, its head, which is most likely the same place where God appeared to him the first time and gave him the commandments.

He also commanded him that no man go up with him, as the first time, such as Aaron and Joshua, because God would appear to him more and give him more blessings, such as the radiance of his face. He also commanded that no one come near the mountain, not even the animals, so that all might feel its awe and holiness. Moses carried out the word of God and went up with the tablets on the mountain.

He stood with him there: Moses stood in the cleft in which God had put him (ch. 33:22). After Moses went up to the top of the mountain, God appeared to him in the form of a great cloud, and then he heard a voice from heaven proclaiming that God had come. This stirs feelings of awe and fear and at the same time longing and love within Moses.

God moved before him in the form of a great cloud, which may have been accompanied by a strong light, and then he heard a voice calling the name of the LORD, and the repetition of this was a confirmation of the presence of God Himself, and declaring the attributes of God, which are: (1) Mercy and tenderness toward His people, and pity and compassion for them.
(2) Longsuffering, for He does not become angry with His people quickly if they err and gives them an opportunity to repent. (3) His gifts are many and never end.
(4) He fulfills His promises.
He will by no means clear the guilty: He will not forgive those who persist in sin, whether fathers or children. The voice continues the attributes of God, saying:
(5) God gives His blessings to His people however large their number, whether in the same generation or in the following generations.
(6) God is forgiving to all who repent, whatever their sins.
(7) God is just, so He does not forgive the one who does not repent and persists in sin, and He punishes the children and grandchildren if they walk in the sins of their fathers.

Enjoy the mercies of God, for He is tender beyond all imagination, and seize every opportunity for repentance, and do not be lax with any sin however small, and do not justify it, because He is also just.
If now I have found grace in Your sight: since I have found grace in Your sight.
Moses felt the fear of God and the greatness of His love, so he showed his submission to Him by bowing down on behalf of himself and all his people, and asked of God:

(1) That He go in the midst of His people and bear with their obstinacy and disobedience and give them an opportunity to repent. (2) That He forgive the sins of his people because they felt their sin.
(3) That He have compassion on His people and accept to be King over them.

When God found Moses' response, He promised him not only forgiveness and mercy but the doing of great and awesome wonders, such as their crossing the Jordan River and victory over the peoples dwelling in the land of Canaan. Thus God renewed His covenant with His people.
God declared His covenant with His people with His many blessings mentioned in His previous attributes, and as for the people, their undertaking appears in the following:
(1) Not making a treaty with the wicked inhabitants of the land in Canaan, lest the children of God mingle with them and be defiled by their evil. This happened, sadly, in the days of the Judges.
Their pillars (sacred stones): stone pillars set up for the pagan gods.
Their wooden images (Asherim): wooden poles set up on the high places for the gods of the sky, such as the stars.

(2) Tearing down the altars and the pillars and cutting down the wooden images, as a rejection of pagan worship, because the children of Israel worship God, and He is jealous over them like a bridegroom over his bride, and He is very angry if they mix His worship with their worship of idols.

(3) Not making a treaty with the wicked, lest they mingle with them and flatter them and so take part in the worship of their idols and eat what is sacrificed to them, and by this commit spiritual adultery by leaving the worship of God and turning to the worship of idols.
(4) Not letting their sons marry pagan women, lest they draw them into the worship of idols and so they fall into spiritual adultery.
(5) He warned them against imitating the pagans in making images and worshiping them.

(6) He stressed to him some positive laws that He had mentioned to him the previous time when He gave him the two tablets, so He reminded him to keep the feast of the Passover and the days of Unleavened Bread that follow it, seven days, that is, the feast of Unleavened Bread at the beginning of the seven days and at their end, as was mentioned before (ch. 12), in sanctification of their coming out of the land of Egypt in the month of Abib.

(7) He also reminded him of the law of redemption, because God killed the firstborn of Egypt and redeemed the firstborn of His people. So every firstborn is offered to God, and likewise the firstborn of the animals, except the donkey, which is redeemed with a lamb (ch. 13). Thus he does not appear before God empty-handed but offers his gifts to God. This was explained before in (ch. 23).
(8) He reminded him to keep the law of the Sabbath, which is the fourth commandment, even if it be in the season of plowing or harvest (ch. 20:4).
(9) He also alerted him to the feasts of Weeks and Ingathering (ch. 23).

(10) He commanded him to keep the three feasts, that is, the Passover, Weeks (Pentecost) and Ingathering (Tabernacles), at which all the males come to celebrate before God. He promised him, if he keeps the commandments of God, the following: (a) The driving out of the pagans, the inhabitants of the land.

(b) He will bless his land and grant him to possess the Promised Land. The borders of the kingdom of the children of Israel were greatly enlarged in the days of Solomon (1 Kgs 4:21), but they shrank when they fell into many sins, and indeed the enemies occupied it completely during the captivity.
(c) None of the pagans will covet or dare to enter his land when his males go up to celebrate the three feasts of God.
(11) He warns him against using leaven at the feast of the Passover or leaving any of its meat until the next day, as was mentioned before in (ch. 12).
(12) He commanded him to bring the firstfruits of his produce to God (ch. 23). (13) He commanded him not to boil a young kid that is still nursing (ch. 23).
If you want to enjoy the mercies of God, you must keep His commandments with all care, and if you err, repent quickly, and then He fulfills all His covenants to you.

God asked Moses to write the laws that He had told him in a book, so that he might teach them to the people and they might not forget them, and might be committed to them, and so keep the covenant of God and receive His blessings.

Moses spent forty days and forty nights with God fasting; he neither ate nor drank during them, and this was by divine help and power. This is the second time of Moses' fasting forty days and forty nights; the first was when he received the two tablets the first time (ch. 24:18), and Elijah fasted the like (1 Kgs 19:18), and then Christ (Mt 4:2). This fast is a miracle that exceeds the capacities of human beings and was accomplished by the power of God. Moses spent this period praying for Aaron and all the people, and God may have stressed to him some commandments and laws that were mentioned before (chs. 21-24), and the design of the tabernacle and its erection (chs. 25-31), and at its end God commanded him to write the Ten Commandments on the two tablets that Moses had made. Notice here that the two tablets the second time were made by Moses and not by God, as a discipline for him because he became angry and in the heat of his anger broke the first two tablets, which God Himself had made. Then God wrote the Ten Commandments on the two tablets with His finger.
Do not fear the difficulty of the commandment or of the spiritual practices of prayers and fasts, because God will give you help to fulfill them and to enjoy in them fellowship with God.

After Moses received the two tablets of the law the second time from God, He gave him a grace, which was that his face shone with a great radiance as a declaration of his righteousness and holiness, so that the people would submit to him and obey the words of God on his tongue. So God adorns His children in every generation with virtues that they do not see, because of their humility, but people notice in them very clearly.

God is ready to give you a special grace so that others may revere and respect you, and you may show them the word of God. Therefore be careful in your speech and remember that you are the voice of God to those around you, so let no evil word come out of your mouth.

Moses came down from the mountain and went to meet the people under the leadership of Aaron, and they were this time waiting for him with care, and were surprised by the radiance of his face and feared greatly and felt the fear of God when he approached them, which made them keep further and further from their sins.

Moses approached Aaron and the leaders of the people, who were in great fear of the radiance of his face, and he spoke to them all that God had commanded him. Then he approached the people, who also feared the brightness of his face, and perhaps they looked at the ground in humility because they could not bear to see the radiance of his face, and he also told them of the commands of God.

Moses did not know that his face was shining, but the people told him of it, and indeed declared that they could not bear to see the radiance of his face and asked him to cover it. So out of pity for them he put a veil or covering on his face when he approached them and taught them. And when he left them and entered the tabernacle of meeting to speak with God, he would remove the veil from his face.

There is another opinion in the interpretation of this part, that Moses, besides removing the veil in his talk with God in the tabernacle, would keep the veil removed when teaching the people so that they might feel the fear of God, and then put it back on his face in his ordinary talk with the people.
St. Paul the Apostle spoke of this veil in (2 Cor 3:7-18) to show that the knowledge of God was still obscure in the Law, but in the New Testament it appeared clearly.

The veil signifies your weakness and your inability to see the works of God and His glory. The more you live a life of repentance, the more you can hear the voice of God and see His works in all the events around you, and you can understand His word in the Holy Bible. Ask for His help in humility, and He will remove from you every barrier that hinders you from sensing Him and understanding Him.
The preparation for the tabernacle of meeting
Engraver: engraving the precious stones and setting them.
Embroiderer: decorating cloth with gold threads by working them into the fabric.
Embroidery: the various works of embroidery in cloth.
He mentions the metals used in the tent under the leadership of Ithamar the priest, the youngest son of Aaron, and with the help of Bezaleel and Aholiab, who were skilled in the various crafts.
Talent: 45 kg of gold.
The shekel: 15 g.
This is the quantity of gold used, and it is very great and equals millions of Egyptian pounds.
Talent: 3000 shekels, and the shekel of silver = 15 g.
The shekel of the sanctuary: an exact shekel kept in the house of the Lord to measure by.
"A bekah for every man": sometimes it is said half and at other times half a shekel, and the former is a kind of abbreviation.

He mentions here the quantity of silver used in the tent. Moses had collected the silver of the ransom for the males of the children of Israel before the tent of meeting was set up, and after the tent was set up a census was made of the number of males twenty years old and upward, and it was found that the amount of silver matched the number of males in the census (Num 1:46, 2:32, 33), and this shows the faithfulness of all the people in offering the silver of the ransom according to God's commands. There is another opinion that Moses also took a census before the tent was set up and collected the silver of the ransom.
He mentions here the quantity of bronze used in the tent.

The concern of the people to give for setting up the dwelling of God among them appears here, to call us to care for the churches and everything in them, for they are the greatest place in the world, where God dwells with His most holy Body and Blood.
The priestly garments
"They did beat": they hammered the gold until it became very thin plates, and by heating they were able to turn them into threads.

entries.section: (4) The glory of the Lord fills the tabernacle

paragraphs.text: After the tent was set up and anointed, the pillar of cloud came down on the tent and covered it, proclaiming God's blessing and His acceptance to dwell in their midst.

entries.section: (4) The glory of the Lord fills the tabernacle

paragraphs.text: Moses was afraid to enter the tent, the dwelling of God, because of His glory and greatness. After a while God allowed them to enter and serve in it by renewing the oil of the lampstand and the showbread and offering the sacrifices on the bronze altar.

entries.section: (4) The glory of the Lord fills the tabernacle

paragraphs.text: When the cloud rose in the sky and moved, the children of Israel journeyed after it, and when it came down they pitched the tent of meeting and their tents around it.

entries.section: (4) The glory of the Lord fills the tabernacle

paragraphs.text: At night the pillar of cloud turned into a pillar of fire before the tent of meeting to give them light.

This pillar was a proclamation of the presence of God in their midst, in addition to its being their leader in their journeys as the Lord commanded, and this pillar was mentioned in detail in (ch. 13:21, 22).

How beautiful it is for God to lead your life, so that you move if He commands you to, and stand if He wishes, and this is by submission to the Church, the Holy Bible and the guidance of the father of confession.

Symbols of the tent of meeting. No. / The symbol / What is symbolized. 1. The tent of meeting in the midst of the camp: Christ incarnate in the midst of His people (Mt 1:23), and the Church or the Kingdom of Heaven (Heb 9:9, 23, 8:5). 2. Gold: divinity and glory. 3. Silver: redemption, because it was collected as a ransom for the males (ch. 30:12, 13), and it also refers to the word of God.
4. Bronze: judgment, since the altar of burnt offering is made of it, with which God the Judge is pleased with His people.

5. Acacia wood: the humanity of Christ, overlaid with gold because of the union of divinity with humanity in Christ. 6. Fine twined linen, that is, linen: the righteousness of Christ, which He gives to His believing children. 7. The color blue: heaven and the heavenly life. 8. The color purple: the kingship of Christ. 9. The color scarlet: the sufferings of Christ and His blood. 10. The hanging at the door of the tent: Christ is the door and the way (Jn 10:9, 14:6). And the Holy Place and the Holy of Holies. 11. The bronze altar of burnt offering: the crucified Christ, who is the way to the Holy of Holies.

12. The laver: Baptism. 13. The boards of the tent overlaid with gold: the believers built up as living stones (1 Pet 2:5), covered by the glory of God. 14. The bars: unity (Eph 4:3). 15. The silver bases of the boards: the redemption on which the Church rests. 16. The colored linen covering of the tabernacle: the beauty of Christ and His virtues that appear in the colors, and His righteousness, which the linen signifies, and on it the Cherubim, that is, the angels who serve Him, and it also signifies the believer adorned with virtues, clothed with righteousness, for whom the angels intercede.

No. / The symbol / What is symbolized. 17. The covering of rams' skins dyed red: the blood of Christ the Redeemer. 18. The covering of goats' hair: the sacrifice of Christ, whom the goats that are slain signify. 19. The covering of badgers' skins: Christ, the Church and the believer, who shows outward weakness but in whom is the power of God. 20. The altar of incense: Christ the Intercessor, who died, that is, was burned, for us. 21. The golden lampstand: the Holy Spirit, who works in Christ and works in the Church and the believers. 22. The table of showbread: the incarnate Christ, who gives us His Body and Blood on the altar. 23. The veil between the Holy Place and the Holy of Holies: sin and enmity, which separate God and man, and which Christ removed by His redemption (the tearing of the veil at the death of Christ). 24. The Holy of Holies: heaven, where the throne of God is and where He dwells in His glory, and it is a cube, so it signifies the Holy Trinity.
25. The ark of the covenant: the presence of God in the midst of His people, and the incarnate Christ, and the Virgin who carried divinity in her womb.

26. The cover: the mercy of God, because the blood is sprinkled on it, so that divine justice, represented in the Cherubim, is satisfied, and it also points to the Virgin, who is overshadowed by the angels.

27. The two tablets of the Law inside the ark: Christ the Word of God. 28. The pot of manna inside the ark: the manna signifies the incarnate Christ and the Body and Blood of Christ, and the Virgin Mary, whom the pot signifies.
29. Aaron's rod that budded: Christ who rose, and the Virgin Mary, who gave birth without seed. The ark: man.
